title: Midterm
notes: Readability: programs should be easy to read.
Writability: programs should be easy to write; programmer time is valuable.
Reliability: programs should behave as intended; language should make accidental bugs harder to introduce.
Reliability is affected by type compatibility checks, array bounds checks, and exception handling.
Efficiency considers run time speed and the behind-the-scenes work required by the language implementation.
Postponing actions from compile time to run time costs speed and often trades efficiency for reliability.
Simplicity: fewer features can be easier to learn but may limit what is easy to express.
Complexity: more features can make tasks easier but increases learning burden and can lead to partial-language use.
Ease of learning is an evaluation criterion distinct from simplicity.
Suitability for a particular task is an evaluation criterion (choose the right language for the job).
Imperative paradigm: program is a sequence of commands that update variables over time.
Functional paradigm: program is built from functions and composition rather than variable updates.
Logic paradigm: program is facts/rules and execution finds solutions that satisfy constraints.
Object-oriented paradigm: classes/objects, inheritance, and information hiding.
Scripting languages are typically dynamically typed and often used to glue tools (including web apps).
Concurrent languages emphasize safe shared-resource access and inter-process communication.
TPK algorithm is used to compare language features across languages (types, arrays, loops, functions, I/O, comments).
FORTRAN: created for mathematical/scientific computation (John Backus, IBM).
COBOL: created for business data processing with English-like phrases.
C: created for Unix and system programming (Dennis Ritchie, Bell Labs).
C++: adds classes to C while preserving backward compatibility with C.
Java: object-oriented C-like language that breaks backward compatibility with C.
Pascal: created primarily as a teaching language (Niklaus Wirth).
Smalltalk: one of the earliest major object-oriented languages (Alan Kay and others).
LISP: historically associated with artificial intelligence and symbolic processing.
Prolog: example of a logic programming language (facts + inference).
Scheme uses prefix notation: (operator operand1 operand2 ...).
Nesting expressions models function composition, e.g., (sin (+ x y)).
quote (or ') prevents evaluation and returns literal data.
car returns the first element of a list; cdr returns the rest of the list.
cons constructs a list from a head element and a tail list.
Common recursion pattern: base case (null? L), recursive step uses (cdr L).
cond selects the first true branch; else/#T is used as a default branch.
Equality predicates differ: = is numeric equality; eq? and equal? compare other kinds of values.
BNF grammars describe syntax (form); semantics is meaning.
BNF grammar components: terminals, nonterminals, a start symbol, and productions (rules).
A derivation starts at the start symbol and applies productions until only terminals remain.
Syntax diagrams are an alternative to BNF for representing syntax (graph-based).
In syntax diagrams used here, rectangle nodes label another graph (like a nonterminal reference).
In syntax diagrams used here, circle nodes represent literal terminals in the string.
EBNF extensions: {...} repetition, [...] optional, and | alternation.

flashcards.front: What does this mean: car
flashcards.back: car returns the first element of a list.

flashcards.front: What does this mean: cdr
flashcards.back: cdr returns the list after removing the first element.

flashcards.front: What does this mean: cadr / caddr
flashcards.back: cadr = second element; caddr = third element (combinations of car/cdr).

flashcards.front: What does this mean: (quote X) / 'X
flashcards.back: Returns X without evaluating it.

flashcards.front: What does this mean: (null? L)
flashcards.back: Checks whether L is the empty list ().

flashcards.front: What does this mean: base case in recursion
flashcards.back: A condition (often (null? L)) that stops recursion and returns a final value.

flashcards.front: What does this mean: cons cell diagram
flashcards.back: A box-and-pointer representation of lists built from pairs; cons links a head to a tail.

flashcards.front: What does this mean: terminal
flashcards.back: A literal symbol that appears in strings of the language (cannot be expanded by rules).

flashcards.front: What does this mean: nonterminal
flashcards.back: A grammar variable that can be expanded using productions (written like <Expr>).

flashcards.front: What does this mean: production
flashcards.back: A rule that rewrites a nonterminal into terminals/nonterminals.

flashcards.front: What does this mean: derivation
flashcards.back: A sequence of rule applications from the start symbol to a terminal string.

flashcards.front: What does this mean: parse tree
flashcards.back: A tree that shows how a string was derived using the grammar’s productions.

flashcards.front: What does this mean: grammar ambiguity
flashcards.back: At least one string has two different parse trees under the grammar.

flashcards.front: What does this mean: EBNF { X }
flashcards.back: { X } means repeat X zero or more times.

flashcards.front: What does this mean: EBNF [ X ]
flashcards.back: [ X ] means X is optional (zero or one time).

flashcards.front: What does this mean: alternation (|)
flashcards.back: In grammar rules, | means choose one of the alternatives.

flashcards.front: What does this mean: backward compatibility (C++ vs C)
flashcards.back: C++ kept C compatibility so many C programs can compile as C++; Java did not.

flashcards.front: What does this mean: teaching language
flashcards.back: A language designed to help novices learn programming concepts (e.g., BASIC, Pascal).

flashcards.front: What does this mean: systems language
flashcards.back: A language designed for low-level/system software (e.g., C for Unix/OS).

flashcards.front: What does this mean: business language
flashcards.back: A language designed for business data processing (e.g., COBOL, FLOW-MATIC).

quiz.question: Which evaluation criterion focuses on how easy a program is to read and understand?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). Readability measures how easily programmers can read and understand code.

quiz.question: Which criterion is most directly described by: “the programmer’s time is valuable; the language should be easy to code in”?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). Writability is about how easy it is to write programs in the language.

quiz.question: Including run-time array bounds checking most directly improves which evaluation criterion?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). Bounds checking helps prevent accidental out-of-bounds bugs, improving reliability.

quiz.question: Postponing work from compile time to run time generally affects performance in what way?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). More work at run time adds overhead, typically slowing execution.

quiz.question: A language that has many different control constructs and many specialized features is usually considered more ____.
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). More features generally increase complexity and learning burden.

quiz.question: Which choice best describes a typical tradeoff discussed in class?
options: Run-time safety checks improve reliability but can reduce efficiency
More features always improve simplicity and efficiency
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). Safety checks add overhead but help catch errors.

quiz.question: The C/C++ pattern `if (x = 4) ...` is an example of language features that can invite mistakes, reducing ____.
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). Accidental assignment in a condition can create subtle bugs (reliability concern).

quiz.question: Which criterion asks whether programs in the language run fast and avoid unnecessary overhead?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). Efficiency focuses on run time speed and resource overhead.

quiz.question: Choosing a language because it is ideal for a specific domain (e.g., business vs scientific) is primarily about ____.
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). Suitability considers how well a language fits the job.

quiz.question: If a language is easier for beginners to learn quickly, that is mainly the criterion of ____.
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). Ease of learning is about how quickly someone can become productive.

quiz.question: FORTRAN was originally designed primarily for which purpose?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). FORTRAN was created for scientific/mathematical programming.

quiz.question: COBOL was designed primarily for which purpose?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). COBOL was created for business data processing and used English-like phrases.

quiz.question: Which language is closely associated with building the Unix operating system?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). C was developed at Bell Labs and used heavily for Unix.

quiz.question: Which language is widely known as being designed for artificial intelligence and symbolic processing?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). LISP is historically associated with AI and symbolic computation.

quiz.question: Which language was developed by adding classes to C while trying to preserve backward compatibility with C?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). C++ extended C with classes and kept backward compatibility.

quiz.question: Which language is described as an object-oriented C-like language that breaks backward compatibility with C?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). Java is C-like but intentionally not backward compatible with C.

quiz.question: Which early language is often credited as one of the earliest object-oriented languages and influenced OO concepts?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). Simula introduced key OO ideas that influenced later OO languages.

quiz.question: Which language was created as a teaching language by Niklaus Wirth?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). Pascal was designed largely for teaching programming.

quiz.question: FLOW-MATIC and COBOL are notable for using what kind of syntax style?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). They emphasized English-like keywords and phrasing for business use.

quiz.question: Ruby is most accurately described as which of the following (in the course materials)?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). Ruby is commonly presented as a pure OO scripting language in the class material.

quiz.question: Evaluate: (car (cdr '(red yellow blue green)))
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). cdr drops the first element (red), then car takes the first of the remainder (yellow).

quiz.question: Evaluate: (caddr '(lime kelly forest mint))
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). caddr = car of cdr of cdr, i.e., the 3rd element of the list.

quiz.question: Evaluate: (cons (car '(purple violet)) (cdr '(orange tangerine)))
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). car gives purple; cdr gives (tangerine); cons builds (purple tangerine).

quiz.question: Given (define (f L) (cond ((null? L) 'troll) ((null? (cdr L)) 'elf) ((> (car L) (* (cadr L) 2)) 'hobbit) (else (f (cdr L)))))  Evaluate: (f '(1 5 9))
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). It skips until L becomes a 1-element list, then returns 'elf.

quiz.question: Using the same f as above, evaluate: (f '(4 13 2 3))
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). From (4 13 2 3), it recurses to (13 2 3). Since 13 > (2*2)=4, the third cond branch triggers and returns 'hobbit.

quiz.question: Which expression returns the empty list in Scheme?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). The cdr of a 1-element list is the empty list ().

quiz.question: Which of the following prevents evaluation and returns the literal data?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). quote returns the expression/list without evaluating it.

quiz.question: Which predicate checks structural equality of lists (not just symbols/identity)?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). equal? compares list structure/content.

quiz.question: What does (and (> 5 3) (< 6 8)) evaluate to?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). Both comparisons are true, so and returns #T.

quiz.question: A correct recursive structure for scanning a list L is usually:
options: Check (null? L) then recurse on (cdr L)
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). Most list recursion uses a base case for empty list and recurses on (cdr L).

quiz.question: In EBNF, what does [ X ] mean?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). [X] denotes an optional part.

quiz.question: In EBNF, what does { X } mean?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). {X} denotes repetition (possibly zero).

quiz.question: A grammar is ambiguous when ____.
options: some string has two different parse trees
two rules share the same left-hand side
a terminal appears on the left side
the grammar has more than 5 rules
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). Ambiguity is defined by multiple parse trees for at least one string.

quiz.question: In BNF, the start symbol is a ____.
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). The start symbol is the designated nonterminal you begin derivations with.

quiz.question: Which is a correct EBNF rule for an Ada simple loop: loop <statement>; ... end loop; with at least one statement?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). One required statement plus zero-or-more additional statements is captured by <statement>; {<statement>;}

quiz.question: Consider: <Num> -> <Digit><Digit>. Which string is in <Num>?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). <Num> requires exactly two digits.

quiz.question: Using the Practice Exam Duration grammar, which string is derivable?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). The grammar requires <Num>:<Num> with two-digit numbers; 03:30-10:45AM matches.

quiz.question: In syntax diagrams used in this course, a rectangle-shaped node typically indicates ____.
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). Rectangles label other graphs (like nonterminals).

quiz.question: In syntax diagrams used in this course, a circle-shaped node typically indicates ____.
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). Circles correspond to literal terminals to be matched in the input string.

quiz.question: If a grammar has productions like A -> a c and A -> c a, then which string is in the language of S -> A A?
quiz.explanation: Source: New (Midterm Coverage). Choose A->ac then A->ca to get acca.
